a: Once again the Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD
t: The last cycle, and the broken pattern
p: The familiar opening returns one last time, but this time Israel never cries out to God.
b: Each earlier story ran the same course: Israel does evil, God hands them over, Israel cries out, God raises a rescuer (see 3:7–9; 6:1–7; 10:6–10). Here the first two steps come, but the third never does. No one in Israel asks for help, and in chapter 15 the men of Judah even hand their rescuer over to the enemy. Readers who follow the book's downward slide (the L lens) take this as the clearest sign that the cycle itself is breaking down. God still sends a rescuer, unasked, and even he will only begin the work (13:5).

a: handed them over to the Philistines for forty years
p: The longest oppression in the book. The Philistines held the coastal plain and pushed into Israel's foothills.
b: The Philistines settled the southern coast early in the 1100s BC (see the topic page). Their five cities lay on the plain; the Shephelah, the low hills between the plain and Judah's mountains, was the contested border zone. Every place in the Samson stories (Zorah, Eshtaol, Timnah, the Sorek Valley, Lehi) lies in or near that zone. The forty years are not closed off in Judges: the Philistine threat runs on through Eli and Samuel (1 Samuel 4–7) and is broken only under David (2 Samuel 5:17–25; 8:1).

a: In Zorah lived a man named Manoah, from the clan of the Danites
p: Zorah sat on a ridge above the Sorek Valley, on the edge of Philistine country.
b: Zorah (modern Tel Tzora) and Eshtaol were among the towns given to Dan (Joshua 19:41). Dan's territory reached down toward the coast, but the tribe was hemmed into the hills (1:34), and in chapter 18 most of Dan leaves for the far north. Samson's family belongs to those who stayed. The Hebrew calls Dan here a mishpachah, a "clan," not a tribe, perhaps because only a remnant was left in the south. Jacob's blessing pictured Dan as a snake that brings down horse and rider (Genesis 49:17), and Moses called Dan "a lion's cub" (Deuteronomy 33:22). Samson fits both.

a: His wife was barren
p: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah and Elizabeth: when Scripture says a woman cannot have children, a special son is coming.
b: The pattern runs through the Bible: Sarah (Genesis 11:30), Rebekah (Genesis 25:21), Rachel (Genesis 29:31), Hannah (1 Samuel 1:2), the Shunammite woman (2 Kings 4:14) and Elizabeth (Luke 1:7). In each case the birth shows that the child is God's gift. Manoah's wife is the main actor in this chapter, yet she is never named. Later tradition gave her names: Pseudo-Philo, a Jewish retelling from the first century AD, calls her Eluma (chapter 42), and the Talmud calls her Hazzelelponi (Bava Batra 91a), borrowing the name from 1 Chronicles 4:3.
r: Genesis 11:30; Genesis 25:21; Genesis 29:31; 1 Samuel 1:2; 2 Kings 4:14; Luke 1:7; 1 Chronicles 4:3

a: The angel of the LORD appeared to the woman
t: Who is the angel of the LORD?
p: The visitor is called a man, the angel of the LORD and finally God himself. Readers have long asked who he is.
b: In Hebrew mal'akh means "messenger." In this chapter the woman calls him "a man of God" (13:6), the narrator calls him "the angel of the LORD," and Manoah ends by saying "It is God we have seen" (13:22). Many Jewish readers take him as a created angel who speaks for God. Many Christian readers since Justin Martyr have taken the angel of the LORD as the Son of God appearing before he became human. Many critical scholars think the figure was a way of speaking about God's presence without saying God was seen directly. The text keeps all three possibilities open on purpose.

a: Do not drink wine or other strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean
t: The mother keeps the Nazirite rules
p: The rules of Numbers 6 fall first on the mother: while she carries him, she lives like a Nazirite too.
b: The Nazirite law says the person "must keep away from wine and other strong drink" (Numbers 6:3) and lets "no razor" touch the head (Numbers 6:5). Here the angel lays the wine rule and a ban on unclean food on the woman herself. The child shares her body, so she shares his vow. "Strong drink" (shekhar) is beer or other fermented drink, not distilled liquor. "Unclean" food means the animals forbidden in Leviticus 11, which every Israelite was to avoid. The point is extra care, not a new law.

a: No razor is to touch his head
p: The words echo the Nazirite law, but Samson's vow is lifelong and chosen for him, not taken for a time.
b: Numbers 6 describes a vow that an adult takes for a set period: "no razor is to touch his head" (Numbers 6:5) until the time is over, and then the hair is shaved and offered. Samson's case is different in three ways: God chooses it before birth, it lasts his whole life, and the angel names only the razor, not wine or the dead. Hannah makes a similar promise about Samuel (1 Samuel 1:11), and a Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel (4QSam-a) calls Samuel a Nazirite outright. The Mishnah later spoke of "a Samson-Nazirite," a lifelong vow with its own rules (Mishnah Nazir 1:2; see the note on 14:9).

a: God's Nazirite
p: Nazir comes from a root meaning "to separate, set apart." A related word, nezer, means a crown, and the long hair was the crown.
b: A nazir is someone "separated" or "dedicated." Joseph is called nezir among his brothers, the one set apart (Genesis 49:26). The related noun nezer means both "dedication" and "crown" (Exodus 29:6), and Numbers 6:7 calls the uncut hair "the nezer of his God" on his head. So the hair was the visible sign of belonging to God. "Nazirite" has nothing to do with Nazareth or with the name "Nazarene" in the New Testament, though some early Christians connected them (see Matthew 2:23).

a: He is the one who will begin to rescue Israel
p: Samson will begin the rescue. Samuel, Saul and David must finish it.
b: No other judge's birth is announced, yet the promise is the smallest in the book: he will begin to rescue. Samson kills many Philistines but never frees Israel; at his death the Philistines still rule (15:11; 16:31). The work goes on under Samuel (1 Samuel 7:13), Saul (1 Samuel 14) and David (2 Samuel 5:17–25). Traditional readers see God's plan unfolding step by step. Literary readers see the book lowering expectations: even the most gifted judge only starts what he should finish.

a: A man of God came to me
p: In the Bible a "man of God" is usually a prophet. The woman sees something more but does not know what.
b: The title is used for Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), Samuel (1 Samuel 9:6), Elijah and Elisha (1 Kings 17:18; 2 Kings 4:9). The woman takes the visitor for a prophet, yet says he looked like "God's angel, truly frightening to see." The word for frightening (nora') is used of God himself (Deuteronomy 7:21). She is closer to the truth than her husband, who goes on calling him "the man" (13:11). This gap between what the wife sees and what the husband grasps runs through the chapter.

a: to his dying day
t: What the mother adds and leaves out
p: Retelling the message, she drops the razor and adds "to his dying day." Many readers hear a hint of how the story will end.
b: Compare 13:5 with 13:7. The angel spoke of the razor and of rescuing Israel. The woman leaves out both and adds that the boy will be a Nazirite "to his dying day." Some take this simply as a mother's natural retelling. Many literary readers (Alter, Exum) think the narrator is foreshadowing: the razor will be the secret of the story, and Samson's Nazirite life will end only with his death in 16:30.

a: Oh, Lord, please
p: Manoah prays for the visitor to come back, this time to "us." God answers, but sends the angel to the woman again.
b: The phrase bi adonai is a polite opening, "Please, my lord." Manoah's request is reasonable and pious, and God hears it (13:9). Yet the angel comes again to the woman, alone in the field, and Manoah must be fetched. Feminist and literary readers (Exum, Alter, Adele Reinhartz) note that the husband keeps asking for information his wife already has, and the angel keeps sending him back to her words (13:13–14). Traditional readers see Manoah as a sincere father who wants to raise the child well. Both readings fit the text.

a: what will be the rule for the boy, and what is he to do?
t: The boy's rule and his work
p: Mishpat here is the boy's rule of life. Manoah asks for a plan; the angel only repeats the mother's rules.
b: Mishpat usually means "judgment" or "ruling," but here it is the boy's proper way of life, the rule he lives by (as in 2 Kings 1:7, "what kind of man"). His "work" or "deeds" (ma'aseh) is what he will do. The angel does not answer the question. He repeats what the woman must do (13:13–14), as if to say the boy's future is not Manoah's to manage.

a: Even if you keep me here, I will not eat your food
t: The meal that becomes an offering
p: Like Abraham and Gideon, Manoah offers a meal to a heavenly visitor. Here the meal must become a burnt offering.
b: Abraham's three visitors ate the meal he set before them (Genesis 18:8). Gideon's visitor turned the meal into an offering by touching it with fire (6:19–21). Here the angel refuses to eat and points the meal toward the LORD. The narrator adds that Manoah "did not know" who he was: he is still treating the visitor as an honored human guest. The scene teaches that worship belongs to God alone, a point Revelation makes when an angel refuses John's bow (Revelation 22:8–9).

a: It is wonderful, beyond grasping
t: "Wonderful": a name that cannot be told
p: Pil'i means wonderful, beyond human reach. The same root names the coming child in Isaiah 9:6, "Wonderful Counselor."
b: The adjective pil'i (or peli) comes from pele', "a wonder," something only God can do (Exodus 15:11, "maker of wonders"). Jacob also asked his night visitor's name and was told, "Why is it that you ask my name?" (Genesis 32:29). Isaiah 9:6 calls the promised child Pele' Yo'ets, "Wonderful Counselor" (literally "Wonder of a Counselor"). Many Christian readers link the three passages and see the Son of God here. Jewish readers see an angel guarding the mystery of God. The word may be a description ("it is too wonderful") rather than a name; the verse can be read either way.

a: And something wonderful was done
p: The Hebrew says only "and doing wonders," with no subject. Translations supply the angel or the LORD.
b: The phrase umafli la'asot is a participle with no subject: "and doing a wonder." The KJV supplies "the angel did wondrously." Others read it with the line before: Manoah offered it "to the LORD, who works wonders." The Greek translation, the Septuagint, has a fuller text that names the LORD as the wonder-worker. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew's openness. Whoever is meant, the word picks up the angel's "wonderful" name in 13:18: the wonder that follows (13:20) is the answer to Manoah's question.

a: the angel of the LORD rose with it, up in the altar's flame
p: The visitor goes up with the smoke of the offering. His leaving shows who he was.
b: The angel does not walk away; he goes up in the fire of the altar, as the offering itself "goes up" (the Hebrew word for burnt offering, olah, means "what goes up"). The sight explains Manoah's fear in 13:22. Christian readers have connected the scene with Christ's own offering and ascension. Jewish readers note that the angel's leaving in the flame proved the offering was accepted, which is exactly the wife's argument in 13:23. Elijah later goes up in a whirlwind with chariots of fire (2 Kings 2:11).

a: It is God we have seen!
p: Manoah fears the old rule that no one can see God and live. His wife answers with better theology.
b: God told Moses that "no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20). Yet Jacob said, "I have seen God face to face, and still my life was rescued" (Genesis 32:30), and Gideon too feared death after seeing the angel of the LORD (6:22–23). Manoah calls the visitor elohim, "God." Whether he means God himself or a divine being is debated (the word can mean either). His wife reasons from what God has done: a God who accepted their offering and made them a promise does not mean to kill them.

a: But his wife answered him
p: Jewish and Christian readers, and feminist scholars too, have long noticed that Manoah's wife understands more than he does.
b: She sees the visitor first, both times. She grasps his nature, keeps his rules, and in this verse calms her husband with sound reasoning. Feminist readers such as Exum and Reinhartz see the chapter as quietly reversing the usual order of husband and wife. Traditional Christian readers see a model of faith that reasons from God's promises. All agree she is the one who names the child (13:24).

a: she named him Samson
p: Shimshon comes from shemesh, "sun." Beth-shemesh, "House of the Sun," lay just across the valley.
b: The name Shimshon most likely means "sun-like" or "little sun." Beth-shemesh, a town named for the sun, was a few miles from Zorah (Joshua 15:10; 1 Samuel 6:9). The name does not prove sun worship; place and personal names were often old and common. In the 1800s some scholars read Samson as a sun god in human form, with his hair as the sun's rays and his blinding as sunset. Few hold that today: the stories are full of local places and human detail. Some readers contrast Samson, "sun," with Delilah, whose name sounds like laylah, "night."

a: began to prod him
p: Pa'am means to strike or push, like a bell's clapper or a hammer's beat. The Spirit starts to drive him.
b: The verb pa'am is rare. It is used of a troubled spirit (Genesis 41:8; Daniel 2:1), and its noun means a beat or step. The image is of the Spirit pushing Samson, again and again, toward action. Elsewhere the Spirit "came on" Othniel and Jephthah (3:10; 11:29) and "put on" Gideon like clothing (6:34). With Samson the Spirit "swept down" in sudden bursts (14:6, 19; 15:14). Christians have read these as early signs of the Holy Spirit's work; Jewish readers speak of a spirit of strength or courage given for a task.

a: Mahaneh-dan
p: Mahaneh-dan means "Dan's Camp." 18:12 gives the reason for the name and puts it near Kiriath-jearim.
b: This verse places Dan's Camp "between Zorah and Eshtaol"; 18:12 places it "west of Kiriath-jearim," several miles to the east. Either the Danites camped more than once, or the name stuck to an area rather than a single spot. The name links Samson's story to the Danite migration in chapter 18, which may be earlier in time than Samson even though it comes later in the book.

a: Samson went down to Timnah
p: Timnah is Tel Batash in the Sorek Valley, a town with Philistine-period remains, about four miles from Zorah.
b: Excavations led by George Kelm and Amihai Mazar (1977–1989) found Philistine pottery and buildings in the town's Iron Age levels. Joshua named Timnah on Judah's northern border (Joshua 15:10) and among Dan's towns (Joshua 19:43), but by Samson's day it was Philistine. The Timnah that Judah visited (Genesis 38:12–13) is often thought to be a different town, in Judah's hill country (Joshua 15:57). "Went down" is accurate: the road drops from the ridge at Zorah to the valley floor.

a: and in Timnah he saw a woman
p: He goes down to Timnah, down to the vineyards, down to Ashkelon, down to Etam, and at last down to Gaza in chains.
b: The verb "go down" (yarad) follows Samson through his story (14:1, 5, 7, 10, 19; 15:8, 11; 16:21, 31). Many readers see a pattern that is moral as well as physical: each step takes him further from his calling, until the Philistines "took him down to Gaza" (16:21). It also matters that he "saw" her. Samson is led by his eyes (14:1–3; 16:1), and the Philistines will take his eyes (16:21). The Mishnah drew the lesson: "Samson went after his eyes, so the Philistines put out his eyes" (Mishnah Sotah 1:8).

a: that you go and take a wife from the Philistines, the uncircumcised?
p: Most of Israel's neighbors practiced circumcision. The Philistines, newcomers from the Aegean world, did not.
b: Egyptians, Edomites, Ammonites and Moabites circumcised (Jeremiah 9:25–26), so "uncircumcised" became Israel's special insult for the Philistines (15:18; 1 Samuel 17:26; 31:4). The law forbade marriage with the peoples of Canaan: "Do not marry into their families" (Deuteronomy 7:3). The Philistines are not in that list, but the parents' objection goes to the same fear of being drawn to other gods (Exodus 34:16). Samson's parents speak like faithful Israelites. Their son does not listen.

a: She is right in my eyes.
p: Samson's words sound the theme of the book's ending: everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes.
b: The Hebrew hi yashrah be'enai, "she is right in my eyes," uses the same words as the refrain in 17:6 and 21:25. Moses had warned against just this: "each of us doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (Deuteronomy 12:8). Samson is a preview of the whole people in chapters 17–21: gifted, chosen, and led by what pleases him. The Talmud makes the link with his blinding (Sotah 9b; Mishnah Sotah 1:8): he followed his eyes, and lost them.

a: His father and mother did not know this was from the LORD
t: God at work through Samson's desire
p: The narrator says the marriage plan came from the LORD. Readers answer the hard questions this raises in different ways.
b: The "he" who looks for a pretext could be the LORD or Samson; the Hebrew allows both, but the nearest subject is the LORD. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers see God's providence: God works through human choices, even foolish ones, as with Joseph's brothers (Genesis 50:20) and Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:15). That does not make Samson's choice right. Others read it more sharply: the God of Judges uses a flawed hero because Israel itself has given up the fight (15:11). Critical scholars often see an editor's comment that turns an old folk tale into a story of God's plan.

a: They reached the vineyards of Timnah
p: A Nazirite was to eat nothing from the grapevine. Samson's story keeps bringing him to vineyards.
b: The Nazirite law bans not only wine but grapes, raisins and anything "the grapevine produces" (Numbers 6:3–4). The story places Samson among the vineyards of Timnah, then at a drinking feast (14:10), then in the Sorek Valley, named for a choice grape (16:4). The Bible does not say he ate or drank there. But the setting is pointed. Later rabbis had a saying for Nazirites: "Go around, go around; do not come near the vineyard" (Bavli Shabbat 13a).

a: The Spirit of the LORD swept down on him
p: Tsalach means to rush or burst through. It is used of the Spirit on Samson, on Saul and on David.
b: The verb tsalach with the Spirit appears only in Judges and 1 Samuel: Samson (14:6, 19; 15:14), Saul (1 Samuel 10:6, 10; 11:6) and David (1 Samuel 16:13). It describes a sudden surge of power for a task, not a lasting change of character. Samson's strength is always the Spirit's gift, never simply his own. Christian readers see a preview of the Spirit's power at Pentecost, while also noting the difference: in the Old Testament the Spirit came on chosen individuals for a time, as Joel 2:28 looks forward to the Spirit poured out on all.

a: he ripped the lion apart
p: Strongman heroes who kill lions bare-handed appear in Greek, Mesopotamian and Israelite stories. Is there a link?
b: Heracles strangled the Nemean lion; Gilgamesh and the hero on many Mesopotamian seals wrestle lions; David and Benaiah killed lions too (1 Samuel 17:34–36; 2 Samuel 23:20). Scholars have listed other likenesses between Samson and Heracles: superhuman strength, a fatal weakness tied to a woman, a death that brings others down with him. Some think the Philistines, who came from the Aegean world, carried Greek-style hero tales with them. Most scholars conclude that these are shared folk motifs of the ancient Mediterranean, not borrowing from one story to another. The Bible's distinct point is that Samson's strength comes from the Spirit of the LORD.

a: he found a swarm of bees inside it, and honey
p: Bees do not nest in rotting flesh, but in a dry hollow skeleton they might. Beekeeping in Israel is well attested.
b: Time had passed ("after a while," literally "after days"), so the carcass had likely dried out in the heat. Ancient writers believed bees could be born from a dead animal; Virgil tells of bees bred from a bullock's body (Georgics 4). The Bible does not say that; it says the bees had made a hive inside. At Tel Rehov in the Jordan Valley, archaeologists found a large apiary of clay hives from the 900s BC, the oldest known in the Near East. Honey was a sign of the good land (Exodus 3:8).

a: He did not tell them the honey had come out of a dead lion's body
p: Touching a carcass made a person unclean. Samson hides where the honey came from. Readers disagree on how serious that was.
b: The Nazirite law forbids coming near "anyone who has died" (Numbers 6:6), meaning a human corpse. An animal carcass made anyone unclean until evening (Leviticus 11:39–40), and Samson gave the honey to his parents without telling them. Some readers see the first of Samson's broken vows: wine country, a dead body, and later a drinking feast and a fresh jawbone (15:15). Others point out that the angel stressed only the razor (13:5). The Mishnah takes this second view: a "Samson-Nazirite" may not cut his hair but may become unclean from the dead (Mishnah Nazir 1:2).

a: Samson put on a feast there
p: A mishteh was a feast with drinking. A wedding feast lasted seven days, as with Jacob and Leah.
b: The noun mishteh comes from the verb "to drink." Wedding feasts ran a week (14:12, 17; Genesis 29:27). The text does not say Samson drank, but a Nazirite hosting a drinking feast is pointed, and many readers count it with the vineyards and the carcass. The marriage also seems unusual: the bride stays in her father's house and Samson visits her (15:1). Some scholars compare a kind of marriage known in later Arab custom in which the wife remained with her family; others think the marriage was simply never completed after Samson stormed off (14:19).

a: Let me pose a riddle for you
p: A chidah is a riddle or puzzling saying. Riddle contests were a feast-time game, and this one had high stakes.
b: The Queen of Sheba tested Solomon with riddles (1 Kings 10:1), and wisdom included understanding "what the wise say and the riddles they pose" (Proverbs 1:6). Riddles were popular at feasts across the ancient world. Samson's riddle is unfair, since no one else knew about the lion. The prize is large: a sadin was a fine linen wrap (Proverbs 31:24; Isaiah 3:23), and "sets of fine clothes" were festal outfits (Genesis 45:22; 2 Kings 5:5). Thirty of each was a small fortune.
r: 1 Kings 10:1; Proverbs 1:6; Proverbs 31:24; Isaiah 3:23; Genesis 45:22; Psalm 78:2; 2 Kings 5:5

a: Out of the eater, food came out
p: In Hebrew the riddle is six short words with a ringing sound. Some think it also hides a second, sexual meaning.
b: The Hebrew reads meha'okhel yatsa ma'akhal / ume'az yatsa matoq: "from the eater came food, from the strong came sweet." The lion is the eater and the strong one; the honey is the food and the sweetness. Scholars such as James Crenshaw have suggested that, at a wedding, the guests might first have heard a bawdy double meaning, and that the men's reply (14:18) may itself be a known riddle whose answer is "love." These are proposals, not certainties. On its face, the riddle can be solved only by someone who saw the lion.
orig: מֵהָאֹכֵל יָצָא מַאֲכָל וּמֵעַז יָצָא מָתוֹק

a: Lure your husband into telling us the riddle
p: Pattah means to coax or entice. The Philistines use the same word with Delilah. The story is being set up to repeat.
b: The verb pattah means to persuade by charm or deceit (Exodus 22:16; Proverbs 1:10; Hosea 2:14). The rulers will say the same word to Delilah (16:5). Both women wear Samson down, one for "the seven days" of the feast (14:17), the other "day after day" (16:16), and both times he gives in. The pattern teaches the reader to see the end coming, even when Samson does not.

a: we will set fire to you and to your father's household
p: The threat is carried out in 15:6, after she has done what they asked.
b: She gives the Philistines the answer, and it does not save her. When Samson burns their fields, the Philistines "set fire to her and to her father" (15:6), the very fate they threatened. Feminist readers (Exum, Bal) see her as a woman with no good choice, caught between her own people's violence and her husband's anger. The story also shows how violence spirals: riddle, threat, revenge, counter-revenge, slaughter (14:19–15:8).

a: Samson's wife wept over him
p: She is never named. Readers judge her differently: a betrayer, a victim, or a woman with impossible loyalties.
b: Traditional readers often count her the first of Samson's treacherous women. Feminist readers stress the threat she is under (14:15) and her charge that Samson does not trust her: he has told his parents nothing, and he will not tell her either. Mieke Bal reads the story around this unnamed woman whose "father's house" is burned. The narrator does not condemn her. He shows a marriage built on Samson's "eyes" (14:3) with no trust in it.

a: before the sun went down
t: Before sunset, or before the bridal chamber?
p: The word for sun here is an unusual one. Some scholars propose a one-letter change: "before he went into the bridal chamber."
b: The text says beterem yavo hacharsah, using cheres, a rare poetic word for the sun (Job 9:7), with an odd ending. Several scholars since the 1800s have suggested reading hachadrah, "into the chamber" (the same word as in 15:1), which would mean the men answered just before Samson entered the bridal room on the last night. No manuscript has that reading, so it remains a guess. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew as it stands.

a: Had you not plowed with my heifer
p: A farmer's insult: you used my animal to do your work. Many hear a sexual slur on the wife as well.
b: A heifer was a young cow; to plow with another man's heifer was to use what was his without asking. The image fits the countryside (compare Hosea 10:11; Amos 4:1). Because plowing was also a picture for sex in the ancient world, many readers hear Samson accusing the men of more than cheating. Either way, he speaks of his wife as livestock. His reply rhymes in Hebrew, matching their riddle-answer with one of his own.

a: Down he went to Ashkelon and struck thirty men of theirs dead
p: The Spirit empowers Samson to pay his debt by killing strangers. How can that be?
b: Ashkelon lay over twenty miles away on the coast, one of the five Philistine cities. Samson pays his wager with clothes taken from the dead. Traditional readers say the Spirit gave power for Israel's war with an oppressor, even through a man with poor motives; God's purpose (14:4) was being served. Some Christian readers stress that the Spirit's coming did not approve everything Samson did. Critical scholars see an old tale of a trickster-bandit with a pious frame added. Many modern readers find the scene troubling and say the narrator meant it to be.

a: the one who had been his groomsman
p: The companion who stood with the groom at the wedding ends up with the bride.
b: The Hebrew says the companion "had been made a friend" to Samson, a special role at the wedding like a best man. John the Baptist calls himself "the friend of the bridegroom," who rejoices at the groom's voice (John 3:29). Here the friend takes the bride. Her father thinks Samson has left her for good (15:2). He may have believed that left him free to give her to another man.
orig: מֵרֵעֵהוּ אֲשֶׁר רֵעָה לוֹ (mere'ehu asher re'ah lo)

a: during the wheat harvest, Samson came to see his wife, bringing a young goat
t: Wheat harvest and a young goat
p: Wheat was harvested in May and June, when fields were dry. A young goat was a gift for a visit, or a payment.
b: The timing sets up the fire in 15:5: dry standing grain and stacked sheaves burn fast. The young goat is a gift to his wife. In Genesis 38:17 Judah promised a young goat as payment to a woman he took for a prostitute. Some readers hear that echo here, as Samson comes to claim his rights in the bedroom ("her room," the same word as the inner room in 16:9).

a: Isn't her little sister better than she is?
p: Like Laban with Leah and Rachel, the father offers one daughter in place of another.
b: Laban gave Jacob the older sister when he wanted the younger (Genesis 29:23–26). Here the father offers the younger in place of the older. In both stories the daughters have no say. The father's offer is his attempt to calm an angry, dangerous son-in-law, and it fails.

a: captured three hundred foxes
p: Shu'al can mean fox or jackal. Jackals move in packs and would be easier to catch in large numbers.
b: Shu'alim are foxes in Song of Songs 2:15 and Nehemiah 4:3, but many scholars think jackals are meant here, since foxes live alone and three hundred would be hard to gather. Psalm 63:10 speaks of bodies left as food for shu'alim, which fits jackals. The Plain English Translation keeps the familiar "foxes." Tying them in pairs keeps each pair from running straight back to its den, so they zigzag through the fields.
r: Song of Songs 2:15; Nehemiah 4:3; Psalm 63:10; Lamentations 5:18

a: sent the foxes into the Philistines' fields of grain
p: The Roman poet Ovid describes foxes released with burning torches at a spring festival. Is it connected?
b: In his Fasti (book 4), Ovid explains a rite at the Roman Cerealia, the festival of the grain goddess Ceres, in which foxes with lit torches on their backs were let loose. He tells a tale of a boy who wrapped a fox in straw and set it alight, and the fox burned a field of grain. Some scholars have suggested a shared old custom or story behind both accounts. The evidence for a direct link is thin: Ovid wrote a thousand years after Samson's time, and the uses are different (a ritual in Rome, an act of war in Judges). The likeness is real, the connection is unproven.

a: set fire to her and to her father
p: Each side says it is only paying the other back. The women and the father die in the middle.
b: Samson says he will be blameless this time (15:3). The Philistines burn his wife and her father. Samson swears revenge (15:7). Judah's men ask why, and he answers, "As they did to me, so I have done to them" (15:11). The Philistines come "to treat him the way he treated us" (15:10). The story lets every party speak the language of fair payback. The innocent are the ones who burn. The threat of 14:15 has come true despite the wife's compliance.

a: He struck them down, leg upon thigh, a great slaughter
p: An old idiom for a crushing blow. Its exact image is lost. The KJV's "hip and thigh" became an English proverb.
b: The Hebrew shoq al-yarekh is found only here. It may come from wrestling, or from butchering, or picture bodies heaped up with legs over thighs. All agree on the sense: a complete defeat. English took the KJV's "smote them hip and thigh" into everyday speech for a thorough beating.

a: Don't you know the Philistines are our masters?
p: Three thousand men of Judah come, not to fight the Philistines, but to tie up Samson for them.
b: In 1:1–2 Judah led Israel against the Canaanites. Here Judah's men accept Philistine rule as normal and see Samson as the problem. Three thousand men go to arrest one man. Readers of the book's downward slide see Israel no longer wanting to be rescued. Christian readers have often compared the scene with Jesus handed over by his own people to foreign rulers (Matthew 27:1–2), though the comparison is loose. Jewish readers note that Samson does not fight his own people: he lets them tie him (15:12–13).

a: the ropes on his arms turned into flax that people have put to the fire
p: Flax that has been through fire falls apart at a touch. The image matches the burning of 15:5–6.
b: The Philistines burned Samson's wife with fire; now the Spirit makes the ropes like flax in fire. The bonds "dissolved" (literally "melted") from his hands. New ropes (15:13) will appear again in Delilah's tests (16:11–12), and again they will not hold him. Only the loss of the LORD's presence will make him weak.

a: the jawbone of a donkey that had died not long before
p: Teriyyah means moist or fresh: the jaw was from a donkey recently dead, so it was heavy and not brittle.
b: An old dry jawbone would shatter; a fresh one is a solid club with teeth still in it. But a fresh jaw is also unclean flesh, and Samson grabs it without a thought (see the note on 14:9). Shamgar killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad (3:31). Both stories show God giving victory through a farm tool or a bone, not a soldier's weapon. Samson's own boast in 15:16 forgets to mention God at all.

a: a heap, two heaps!
p: Chamor means "donkey," and the same letters mean "heap." Samson's victory song is a pun.
b: The Hebrew reads bilchi hachamor chamor chamoratayim: "with the jaw of the donkey, a heap, two heaps." Some render the pun as "I have made donkeys of them" or "I have piled them in donkey-heaps." The Greek translators read the word as a verb, "I have wiped them out." Short victory chants like this were sung after battles (1 Samuel 18:7). The Plain English Translation keeps "a heap, two heaps" and notes the play on words here.

a: he named that place Ramath-lehi
p: "Jawbone Hill," or by a play on words, "the throwing of the jawbone." Lehi means "jaw."
b: Ramah usually means "height," but the verb ramah means "throw," and Samson has just thrown the jaw away. Lehi itself, "Jaw," may have been named for the shape of a rock or ridge. The place is in Judah near Etam, but its exact site is unknown. 2 Samuel 23:11 may refer to the same place.

a: Am I now to die of thirst and fall into the power of the uncircumcised?
p: Only now, exhausted and thirsty, does Samson speak to God. He gives God credit, and also complains.
b: Samson's prayer begins well: "By your servant's hand you have brought about this great rescue." He calls himself God's servant and calls the victory God's. Then he complains, much as Israel did at Massah when they were thirsty (Exodus 17:1–7). His two prayers in the story both come at moments of weakness (here and 16:28). Readers who see Samson as a man of faith, as Hebrews 11:32 does, point to these prayers. Others note that both are about his own needs.

a: God broke open the hollow at Lehi
p: The KJV's "hollow place that was in the jaw" led many to think water came from the jawbone. Lehi is a place.
b: Makhtesh means a mortar or a hollow shaped like one (Proverbs 27:22; Zephaniah 1:11). Since Lehi means "jaw," and makhtesh can be the socket of a tooth, older readers took the verse to mean that God split a tooth-socket in the jawbone and water flowed from it. The Greek speaks of "the hollow in the jaw," and the Latin Vulgate says God opened "a molar tooth in the jawbone of the donkey." But the text says the hollow is "at Lehi," and the spring is still there "to this day," so a place in the landscape is meant.

a: That is why he named it En-hakkore
p: "The Caller's Spring," named for Samson's call to God. The word can also mean "partridge."
b: Qore' means "one who calls," matching "he called to the LORD" in 15:18. It is also the word for the partridge, a bird known for its call (1 Samuel 26:20). The spring may first have been named for partridges, and the story gives the name a new meaning. Many place names in Judges and Genesis carry this kind of explanation.

a: Samson judged Israel for twenty years
p: The closing formula for a judge appears here and again in 16:31. The story seems to end twice.
b: Usually the book says a judge led Israel for so many years and then died (12:7; 10:2). Here the summary comes before chapter 16. Many critical scholars think chapters 13–15 once formed a complete account, with chapter 16 added later. Literary readers see a pause: Samson's public career is summed up, and then comes the private story of his fall. The phrase "in the days of the Philistines" reminds readers that he judged while the Philistines still ruled.

a: He saw a woman there, a prostitute
p: A wife at Timnah, a prostitute at Gaza, and Delilah. Each time Samson "sees" or "loves," danger follows.
b: The three stories build on each other: the first woman is used against him, the second sets up an ambush, and the third succeeds. The prostitute of Gaza has no lines and no blame; she is part of the trap only by being the place where Samson is found. Gaza, the farthest south of the Philistine cities, is where the story will end (16:21). The rabbis counted Samson's lust as his failing (Sotah 9b), while also honoring him as a judge.

a: carried them up to the top of the hill in front of Hebron
p: Hebron is about forty miles from Gaza and three thousand feet higher. The hill may be one near Gaza that faces toward Hebron.
b: Carrying gates all the way to Hebron would be a feat beyond belief, and many readers think that is the point. Others note that the Hebrew says the hill "on the face of" Hebron, which can mean a hill on the road that faces in Hebron's direction. City gates were heavy wooden doors with a crossbar, set between stone towers. To take a city's gate was to take its strength (Genesis 22:17).

a: tore them loose, bar and all
t: Samson and the gates of death
p: Medieval Christians read Samson carrying off Gaza's gates as a picture of Christ breaking out of the tomb.
b: The enemy waited for morning to kill him (16:2), but he rose at midnight and walked off with the gates. The Biblia Pauperum, a medieval picture Bible, set this scene next to the Resurrection, and church windows and carvings did the same. Typology like this does not claim the author of Judges had Christ in mind; it reads the story as one in a pattern of God's deliverances. Jewish readers take the scene as a sign of the Spirit's strength resting on Samson even in a sinful hour.

a: Delilah was her name
p: The only named woman in Samson's story. Her name's meaning and her people are both uncertain.
b: Delilah may come from a root meaning "to hang down" (of hair or of weakness), or from an Arabic word for flirtation, or it may echo laylah, "night," against Samson's "sun." The text never says she was a Philistine; the Sorek Valley was border land, and her name is Semitic. Traditional readers often assume she was Philistine; some scholars argue she was an Israelite, which would make her betrayal sharper. The text gives her no family, no husband and no city. She acts for herself.

a: the Sorek Valley
p: The Sorek, "choice vine," runs from the hills near Jerusalem past Zorah and Timnah to the sea. It is Samson's home ground.
b: Today it is Nahal Sorek. Zorah and Eshtaol overlook it from the north, Beth-shemesh from the south, and Timnah lies in it further west. Sorek is the name of a fine red grape (Isaiah 5:2; Jeremiah 2:21). A Nazirite in love in the Valley of the Choice Vine: the setting again plays on Samson's vow.

a: Each of us will give you eleven hundred pieces of silver
p: Five rulers times eleven hundred is fifty-five hundred shekels, a huge sum. Micah's mother has exactly eleven hundred in 17:2.
b: A shekel was a weight, about 11 grams (0.4 ounce), not a coin. Five thousand five hundred shekels would be over 60 kilograms (about 130 pounds) of silver. For comparison, a Levite in 17:10 is paid ten pieces a year, and Joseph was sold for twenty (Genesis 37:28). The same odd sum, eleven hundred, opens the next story (17:2). Many readers think the repetition is deliberate, linking Samson's fall with Micah's idol.

a: We want to tie him up and bring him low
p: 'Innah means to humble, overpower or abuse. The same verb is used for what is done to women in 19:24 and 20:5.
b: The rulers want to tie Samson up "to humble him" (le'annoto). Delilah repeats the phrase (16:6), and in 16:19 "she began to bring him low." The verb is 'innah, used of oppressing Israel in Egypt (Genesis 15:13) and of sexual violence against women: Dinah (Genesis 34:2), Tamar (2 Samuel 13:14), and the Levite's concubine (19:24; 20:5), where this translation renders it "dishonor." Samson, who used women, is himself "humbled" by one.

a: seven new cords of gut that have not yet dried out
p: Yeter is a cord of animal gut or sinew, used for bowstrings and tent ropes. Fresh, they are moist and strong.
b: The same word means a bowstring in Psalm 11:2 and a tent cord in Job 4:21. Cords of gut grew stiff as they dried, so fresh ones would be tighter and harder to break. Seven, the number of completeness, recurs: seven cords, seven braids (16:13, 19), seven days of the wedding (14:12). Samson is playing with the truth: the first two tests sound like magic, the third comes close to his hair.

a: as a strand of tow breaks at a whiff of fire
t: Tow at a whiff of fire
p: Tow is the short, rough flax fiber left after combing. It burns at once. The Hebrew says "when it smells fire."
b: Ne'oret appears again in Isaiah 1:31, where the strong will become "tow" and burn. The Hebrew says the cords snapped "as a thread of tow snaps when it smells fire," a vivid picture the Plain English Translation keeps. The repeated phrase "no one learned what made him strong" builds suspense for the last test.

a: in with the web
t: Weaving his hair into the loom
p: Women wove on upright looms. Delilah weaves his braids into the threads and pins them tight.
b: On an ancient loom, the warp threads hung or stretched from a beam, and the weaver beat the cross threads tight with a wooden pin or batten (yated). Samson's long hair, worn in seven braids, could be worked into the warp like thread. Weaving was women's work (Proverbs 31:19; 2 Kings 23:7). Samson pulls out "the pin of the loom, and the web with it" (16:14), the whole loom ripped from its frame. The test comes closer to the truth: this time it involves his hair.

a: How can you say 'I love you' and keep your heart away from me?
p: The text says Samson loved Delilah. It never says she loved him. Readers judge her in sharply different ways.
b: For most of history she has been the model of the treacherous woman, the femme fatale of paintings and of Milton's Samson Agonistes. Many feminist readers question that picture. J. Cheryl Exum argues the story reflects male fears of women's power and secrets; Mieke Bal reads Delilah as an independent woman who wants to know, and who is honest about what she is doing, since she announces each trap. Traditional readers answer that taking silver to hand a man over to his enemies is betrayal by any measure. The narrator gives Delilah no motive except the money.

a: until he was so fed up he could have died
p: The Hebrew says his soul "grew short to death": his patience ran out completely.
b: Wattiqtsar nafsho lamut uses an idiom for impatience, a "short" spirit (Numbers 21:4; Job 21:4; Zechariah 11:8). "To death" makes it extreme. The phrase also foreshadows: the tiredness that makes him tell his secret will end in his death.

a: So he opened his whole heart to her
p: After three traps, Samson must know what Delilah will do. Why does he tell her the truth?
b: Readers give different answers. Some say love blinded him, or he was worn down (16:16). Some say he no longer took his vow seriously and did not believe the LORD would leave him (16:20). Some say he trusted his strength was his own. In Milton's Samson Agonistes, Samson blames himself: he "weakly to a woman must reveal it" (line 50). The Hebrew stresses "his whole heart," the phrase repeated in 16:18. The man who would not tell his wife or parents (14:16) now tells everything.

a: she shaved off the seven braids of his head
p: The Hebrew says she called a man, and "she shaved" the braids. Most take it as "she had him shave."
b: The verb vattegallach is feminine: "she shaved." The man called in may have been a barber she directed, or the Hebrew may simply credit her with what she caused to be done. The KJV reads "she caused him to shave." Some scholars suggest the "man" was one of the men lying in wait. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew's "she shaved off."

a: He did not know that the LORD had left him
p: A common belief says Samson's power was in his hair. The text says it was the LORD's presence. The hair was the sign of the vow.
b: Samson himself says his strength will leave if he is shaved (16:17), and it does. But the narrator explains why: "the LORD had left him." The hair was the visible mark of his dedication to God (Numbers 6:7). Breaking that last part of the vow broke the bond, and the Spirit left him, as it later left Saul (1 Samuel 16:14). When the hair grows back (16:22), Samson does not simply get his power back; he prays for it (16:28).
orig: כִּי יְהוָה סָר מֵעָלָיו (ki YHWH sar me'alav)

a: The Philistines grabbed him and dug out his eyes
p: The Mishnah draws the lesson in one line: Samson went after his eyes, and the Philistines put out his eyes.
b: Blinding captives was a common way to make a strong prisoner harmless and to shame him (1 Samuel 11:2; 2 Kings 25:7). The rabbis read it as measure for measure: "Samson went after his eyes, so the Philistines put out his eyes" (Mishnah Sotah 1:8). The story told us what Samson "saw" (14:1; 16:1) and what was right in his eyes (14:3). In his last prayer he asks for revenge "for my two eyes" (16:28).

a: grinding grain in the prison house
p: Grinding grain was the work of slaves and women. The hero is made to do the lowest work in the house.
b: Every household ground flour daily with hand mills; the task fell to women and slaves (Exodus 11:5; Isaiah 47:2; Lamentations 5:13). For a warrior it was deep shame. Milton's Samson laments that he is "Eyeless in Gaza at the Mill with slaves" (line 41). The Talmud reads "grinding" with a sexual sense as well, saying the Philistines brought their wives to Samson so they would bear strong children (Sotah 10a), a reading few modern scholars share.

a: the hair of his head started growing back
p: One short verse tells the reader what the Philistines do not notice. The story is not over.
b: The verse is set between Samson's humiliation and the Philistine feast. The Philistines think the matter is closed. The reader is told that time is passing and the sign of the vow is returning. Most interpreters see the regrowth as a sign of grace: God has not finished with Samson. Some see a hint of Samson's renewed faith, which shows itself in his prayer (16:28).

a: their god Dagon
t: Dagon was not a fish god
p: A popular idea says Dagon was half fish. Ancient texts show he was an old Semitic god, likely of grain.
b: Dagan was worshiped long before the Philistines, at Ebla, Mari and Ugarit in Syria; at Ugarit, Baal is called "son of Dagan." The Hebrew word dagan means "grain," which may be linked. The Philistines took him over when they settled in Canaan, and he had temples at Gaza and Ashdod (1 Samuel 5:1–7; 1 Maccabees 10:83–84). The fish-god idea rests on a later folk etymology from the Hebrew dag, "fish," found already in Jerome and spread by medieval commentators. Milton gave it its best-known form in Paradise Lost, book 1, where Dagon is "upward Man / And downward Fish."

a: Our god has put in our hand
p: The Hebrew rhymes on "-enu" ("our"). The Plain English Translation gives it a rhyme too: hand, land.
b: In Hebrew the song reads natan eloheinu beyadenu et oyvenu, ve'et machariv artsenu, va'asher hirbah et chalalenu, five words ending in "-enu." It sounds like a chant meant to be shouted by a crowd. The Philistines credit their god, just as Israel's songs credit the LORD (Exodus 15). The question of the next verses is which god is really in control.

a: Send for Samson so he can make us laugh!
p: Tsachaq means to laugh, play or make sport. The word can also hint at mockery or sexual play.
b: The verb sachaq/tsachaq is the root of Isaac's name ("he laughs"). It can mean to perform (2 Samuel 6:21), to mock (Genesis 21:9), or to fondle (Genesis 26:8; 39:14). The Philistines want a show: the blind strongman stumbling for their amusement. The house they gather in will become his tomb and theirs.

a: let me touch the pillars the building stands on
p: A Philistine temple dug at Tell Qasile, in modern Tel Aviv, had its roof held up by two wooden pillars set close together.
b: In the 1970s Amihai Mazar excavated a Philistine temple at Tell Qasile from the 1100s–1000s BC. Its main hall had two stone bases for wooden pillars, set close together on the room's center line. A strong man standing between them could push on both at once. The find does not prove the Samson story, but it shows that the description fits the way Philistine temples were built.

a: Lord GOD, remember me, please!
p: Samson uses God's full name, Adonai YHWH, shown as "Lord GOD." His last prayer asks God to remember him.
b: Adonai YHWH joins "my Lord" with the divine name; English Bibles print it "Lord GOD" to avoid "Lord LORD." He calls God three ways in one breath: Lord GOD, and then Elohim, "O God." "Remember me" is the cry of people in distress (Jeremiah 15:15; Psalm 106:4; Nehemiah 13:31). The thief on the cross asked Jesus, "Remember me" (Luke 23:42). Samson's request is less noble: he wants revenge. Yet God answers.
orig: אֲדֹנָי יֱהוִה זָכְרֵנִי נָא (Adonai YHWH zokhreni na)

a: let me take one revenge on the Philistines for my two eyes
p: The Hebrew is compact: "revenge, one, from my two eyes." It may mean one act of revenge, or revenge for one of his two eyes.
b: Neqam achat mishte 'enai is most often read "one act of revenge for my two eyes," a single blow. But it can also mean "revenge for one of my two eyes," as if even this great slaughter would pay back only half his loss. The darker reading fits Samson's bitterness. The Plain English Translation keeps both open with "one revenge ... for my two eyes."

a: Let my life end with the Philistines!
p: Samson chooses to die. Augustine, the rabbis, Milton and modern readers have weighed what that means.
b: Augustine argued that Samson's death was not suicide in the sinful sense, because the Spirit, who did miracles through him, secretly commanded it (City of God 1.21). Jewish tradition generally honors him as a judge who died fighting Israel's enemies. Hebrews 11:32 lists him among the heroes of faith. Milton's Samson Agonistes presents his end as a heroic return to God. Some modern readers find the act disturbing: a blind captive taking thousands, including women, with him. The text itself gives God the credit for answering his prayer and judges the result by numbers.

a: laid him in his father Manoah's tomb
p: His family brings the body home. Samson ends in his father's tomb, between Zorah and Eshtaol, where the Spirit first stirred him.
b: The burial place repeats 13:25 word for word: "between Zorah and Eshtaol." The story closes a circle. The family is able to go down to Gaza and take the body, which suggests the Philistines were in no state to stop them. In the New Testament, Hebrews 11:32–34 names Samson among those who were made strong out of weakness, which many take as a reference to this last prayer. Christian readers have often seen Samson's victory in death as a faint picture of Christ's. Jewish tradition remembers him as the last of the major judges before Eli and Samuel.

a: A man named Micah lived in the hill country of Ephraim.
p: Chapters 17–21 have no judge, no enemy nation and no rescue. They show Israel from the inside.
b: The stories of the judges are over. Two long episodes follow: Micah's shrine and the Danites (17–18), and the outrage at Gibeah and the war on Benjamin (19–21). Both begin with a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah and travel through the hill country of Ephraim. Both are framed by the refrain "There was no king in Israel" (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25). The first shows religion going wrong; the second, society. Most scholars, traditional and critical, see these chapters as an epilogue, probably placed here for their theme rather than their date (see the note on 19:1).

a: Micah
p: In 17:1 and 17:4 the Hebrew spells his name Micayehu, "Who is like the LORD?" A man with that name makes an idol.
b: The full name Micayehu asks the question of Exodus 15:11: "Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?" The answer the law expects is "no one," and certainly no image (Deuteronomy 4:15–16). After 17:4 the name is shortened to Micah. Some readers think the narrator drops the divine part of his name once the idol is made; others think the short form is just everyday usage. The irony stands either way.

a: You laid a curse over them, and I heard you say it
p: A public curse on an unknown thief was a way to make him confess. The son hears it and brings the silver back.
b: The law knew "the public curse calling for witnesses" (Leviticus 5:1), spoken so that anyone who knew the truth would come forward. Micah, afraid of his mother's curse, confesses. She answers with a blessing to undo the curse, a common practice in the ancient world. The family scene is ordinary. What they do next is not.

a: to make a carved idol and a cast idol
t: Breaking the second commandment, in the LORD's name
p: She dedicates the silver "to the LORD" to make exactly what the law cursed.
b: The law said "A curse on anyone who makes an idol, carved or cast in metal" (Deuteronomy 27:15), and banned images of God (Exodus 20:4; Deuteronomy 4:15–18). The mother uses the language of pious giving, hakdesh hikdashti, "I hereby set it apart," to fund an image. This is not worship of Baal. It is the worship of the LORD in a forbidden form, like Aaron's calf (Exodus 32:4–5) and Jeroboam's calves (1 Kings 12:28). The mother's curse has been lifted; the law's curse now falls on the household.

a: she took two hundred pieces of it
p: She set apart eleven hundred pieces for the LORD, but only two hundred go to the silversmith.
b: Readers have long puzzled over the order of 17:2–4: the silver is given back twice, and the mother says she will return it to her son but gives it to a smith. Some scholars think a line has been moved. Others read the story as it stands, as a sign of a muddled and half-hearted religion: she vows the whole sum and spends less than a fifth. "Carved idol and cast idol" may name one object (an image of wood covered with metal) or two.

a: a house of God
t: "A house of God" or "a house of gods"?
p: Bet elohim can mean a house of God or a house of gods. Micah's private shrine stands against the true house of God at Shiloh.
b: Elohim is the normal word for God, but it is also the plural "gods." Micah calls his images "my gods" in 18:24. The Plain English Translation keeps "a house of God" because Micah thinks he serves the LORD (17:13), and because 18:31 sets his idol against "the house of God" at Shiloh. Bethel, which means "House of God," will later hold Jeroboam's golden calf (1 Kings 12:29).

a: He made an ephod and household gods
p: An ephod was a priest's vest, sometimes used to ask God questions. Teraphim were household images, also used for divination.
b: The high priest's ephod held the Urim and Thummim for seeking God's answer (Exodus 28:6–30). Gideon made a gold ephod that Israel worshiped (8:27). Teraphim were images that could be small (Genesis 31:34) or as big as a person (1 Samuel 19:13), and were used to seek guidance (Ezekiel 21:21; Zechariah 10:2). Hosea lists ephod and teraphim together as things Israel will live without (Hosea 3:4). Micah's shrine is a do-it-yourself oracle: the Danites will use it to ask God about their journey (18:5).
r: Exodus 28:6–30; 8:27; Genesis 31:19; Genesis 31:34; 1 Samuel 19:13; Hosea 3:4; Ezekiel 21:21; Zechariah 10:2

a: ordained one of his sons
p: To "fill the hand" was the term for ordaining a priest. Micah ordains his own son, though only Aaron's family could be priests.
b: The Hebrew mille' yad, "filled the hand," is the technical phrase for ordination (Exodus 28:41; 29:9; Leviticus 8:33), perhaps from placing the first offerings in the new priest's hands. The law kept the priesthood for Aaron's descendants (Numbers 3:10). Micah, an Ephraimite, makes his son a priest at home. Jeroboam would later do the same on a larger scale (1 Kings 12:31; 13:33).
r: Exodus 28:41; Exodus 29:9; Numbers 3:10; 1 Kings 12:31; 1 Kings 13:33; 17:12; Leviticus 8:33

a: Everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes.
t: "No king in Israel": what does the refrain mean?
p: The refrain frames the book's ending. Readers disagree about whether it praises kings, attacks a king, or warns about kings.
b: The words echo Moses: "each of us doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (Deuteronomy 12:8), a warning about worship at any place one likes. The common reading, held by many traditional and critical scholars, is that the book argues for a king who will enforce God's law. A sharper version (Brettler and others) sees a case for David against Saul: Saul's town Gibeah is the villain, Saul's ally Jabesh-gilead is wiped out, and David's Bethlehem is the first Levite's home (17:7) and a place of warm welcome (19:4–9). Martin Buber saw two books joined together: an anti-king book built on Gideon's refusal (8:23) and Jotham's fable (9:7–15), and a pro-king book, chapters 17–21, to which the refrain belongs. Others, such as William Dumbrell, read the refrain the opposite way: Israel's true king was God, and human kings would not do better, as Kings shows. Christian readers see a longing that only Christ the King fulfills.

a: of Judah's clan, was a Levite
p: Levites had no tribal land. This young man belongs to Judah's clan and is also a Levite. How?
b: Levites lived in towns scattered among the tribes (Joshua 21), and Bethlehem was not one of them. Some scholars think "Levite" here names a job, a trained priest for hire, rather than descent; others think a Levite family could live among Judah and be counted with it. Others read the phrase as marking where he lived, not his ancestry. 18:30 will say he came from Moses' own family. His being "of Judah" may also prepare for 19:1, where another Levite takes a wife from Bethlehem in Judah.
orig: מִמִּשְׁפַּחַת יְהוּדָה וְהוּא לֵוִי (mimmishpachat Yehudah vehu Levi)

a: who was staying there as a foreigner
t: Claude's theory: "a foreigner there" is Gershom
p: My suggestion: the Hebrew "he was staying there," gar-sham, spells the same consonants as Gershom, the Levite's ancestor in 18:30.
b: This is my own suggestion. The verse ends vehu gar-sham, "and he was staying there as a foreigner." Written without vowels, gar-sham (גר שם) has exactly the four consonants of Gershom (גרשם). Moses named his son Gershom because "I have become a foreigner living in an alien land" (Exodus 2:22). The young Levite is not named until 18:30, where he turns out to be "Jonathan, son of Gershom, son of Moses." If the play on words is intended, the narrator spells out his family before naming it, and his rootless wandering (17:8–9) acts out Gershom's name. I have not found this point in the commentaries I checked; a match this close may well be noted elsewhere.

a: Be my father and my priest
p: "Father" was a title of honor for a priest or prophet. Micah gives it to a young man he will treat as a son.
b: Elisha called Elijah "my father" (2 Kings 2:12), and the king of Israel called Elisha the same (2 Kings 6:21; 13:14). Joseph was "a father to Pharaoh," meaning his trusted adviser (Genesis 45:8). Micah offers the title and a salary in one breath, and then the young man becomes "like one of his own sons" (17:11). The Danites will offer him the same title and a bigger congregation (18:19).

a: I will pay you ten pieces of silver a year
p: Ten shekels a year, clothes and food: a modest living wage for a household priest.
b: The law provided for Levites through tithes and offerings (Numbers 18:21–24; Deuteronomy 18:1–8), not private contracts. Ten pieces of silver is small beside the eleven hundred spent on the idol (17:2) or paid to Delilah (16:5). The Hebrew "for the days" probably means "per year" (compare 1 Samuel 27:7). The Levite has become a hired man; the Danites will later outbid Micah (18:19–20).

a: Now I am sure the LORD will treat me well, since I've got a Levite for my priest.
p: Micah thinks the right staff guarantees God's favor. The next chapter proves him wrong.
b: Micah is sincere: he names the LORD and wants a proper Levite. But he treats the Levite like an asset that will make God "treat him well." Within a chapter he will lose idol, priest and all (18:24). Readers across traditions take the verse as a warning against trusting in religious forms. The Talmud, surprisingly, says Micah was not denied a share in the world to come because he gave bread to travelers (Sanhedrin 103b). Even here, the rabbis looked for some good.

a: because until then nothing had come to them by lot as their inheritance
p: Joshua 19 gave Dan land near the coast. Here Dan has none it can hold, so the tribe moves north.
b: Joshua 19:40–46 lists Dan's towns, from Zorah and Eshtaol to the sea, and then admits, "But the territory of the Danites slipped out of their hands" (Joshua 19:47). The Amorites pushed Dan into the hills (1:34), and the Philistines held the coast. This chapter tells the longer version of the move Joshua 19:47 sums up in one verse, where Laish is called Leshem. Samson's family is part of the Danite remnant that stayed behind.

a: sent them to scout the land and look it over
t: A conquest story turned upside down
p: Spies, a report, a march and a victory: the chapter follows the pattern of Israel's conquest, with every part bent.
b: Moses sent spies into Canaan (Numbers 13), Joshua sent spies to Jericho (Joshua 2), and the spies came back with a good report (Numbers 13:27; Deuteronomy 1:25). Abraham Malamat showed how the Danite migration follows this pattern step by step. But here the spies ask a hired priest instead of God's leader, the land is not part of Canaan's promise, and the people attacked are peaceful. Many readers think the parody is the point: Dan acts out the conquest without obedience.

a: they knew the voice of the young Levite
p: Either they knew him personally, or they recognized his southern accent.
b: Both readings are old. Some think the Danites from Zorah had met the Levite from Bethlehem, only a day's walk away. Others take "voice" as accent or dialect: they heard that he was not from Ephraim, as the Ephraimites' speech gave them away at the Jordan (12:6). Either way, their three questions are pointed: who brought you, what are you doing, what have you got here?

a: The road you are taking lies before the LORD.
t: An oracle that can be read two ways
p: Nokhach YHWH means "in front of the LORD": under his approving eye, or under his watchful eye. The priest does not say which.
b: The phrase can mean God approves ("the LORD favors your journey") or simply that God sees it (Proverbs 5:21; Jeremiah 17:16). Many readers note that the priest gives the Danites what they want to hear without checking with God at all; no ephod or lot is mentioned. Like the famous Greek oracle that told Croesus a great empire would fall if he went to war (his own, it turned out), the answer is safe whatever happens.

a: came to Laish
p: Laish lay at the springs of the Jordan below Mount Hermon. Digs at Tel Dan uncovered its long history.
b: Laish is named in documents from Mari in Syria in the 1700s BC. Avraham Biran dug Tel Dan from 1966 to 1999. He found a mudbrick city gate from about 1750 BC, a destruction layer followed by a new settlement in the Iron Age, a large platform he identified as Jeroboam's high place (1 Kings 12:29), and in 1993 the Tel Dan Stele, an Aramaic inscription that mentions the "House of David." The springs here are one of the main sources of the Jordan.

a: No one in the land was doing anything to harm them, and no one held power over them
p: This line is one of the most obscure in Judges. Translations differ widely.
b: Word by word: "and there was none humiliating a thing in the land, possessing restraint." The KJV takes it as "no magistrate ... that might put them to shame." Others read "lacking nothing" (changing one letter of maklim, "humiliating," to a form of a verb meaning "to lack," as in 18:10) and "possessing wealth" (reading otser, "treasure," for etser). The Plain English Translation stays close to the Hebrew as it stands. On any reading the point is the same: Laish was rich, quiet and defenseless.

a: in the Sidonian way
p: Sidon was the leading Phoenician city on the coast. Laish shared its peaceful, trading way of life.
b: The Phoenicians of Sidon and Tyre lived by sea trade more than by war. Laish was some 25 miles inland, cut off by the Lebanon range, so Sidon could not help it (18:28). In the conquest lists, Sidon lay at the edge of the land (Joshua 13:6; 19:28), and Judges 1:31 says Asher never drove out its people. Laish is a soft target with no allies.

a: Go on in and take possession of the land.
p: The scouts use the words of the promise. But Laish was peaceful, far off, and never offered terms.
b: Yarash, "take possession," is Deuteronomy's word for receiving the promised land (Deuteronomy 1:8). Traditional readers note that the far north was within the borders God promised (Numbers 34:7–9; Joshua 13:6), so Dan had a claim. Many modern readers, and some traditional ones (Block), point to the law of war: for a town far away, "When you come near a city to fight against it, offer it peace" (Deuteronomy 20:10). The Danites offer nothing. The narrator twice calls Laish "calm and trusting" (18:7, 27), and his sympathy seems to lie with the victims.

a: made camp at Kiriath-jearim in Judah
p: "Town of Forests," on Judah's border with Benjamin. The ark will later stay there for twenty years.
b: Kiriath-jearim was one of the Gibeonite towns (Joshua 9:17) on the border of Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:9; 18:14). After the Philistines returned the ark, it rested there in Abinadab's house until David brought it to Jerusalem (1 Samuel 7:1–2; 2 Samuel 6:2). The site is usually placed at Deir el-Azar, west of Jerusalem. On "Dan's Camp," see the note on 13:25.

a: So now, think about what you are going to do.
p: The scouts do not say "steal the idol" in so many words. They do not need to.
b: The men who stayed with Micah and took his hospitality (18:2) now plan to rob him. They know exactly what is in the house: ephod, household gods, carved idol and cast idol. The list will be repeated four times in the next verses, like an inventory. The Danites want a god of their own to take north, and Micah's shrine is ready-made.

a: Which is better for you: to be the priest for one man's household, or the priest for a whole tribe
p: The Danites offer a promotion. The priest is happy to go.
b: The Levite does not argue, pray or ask God. "The priest's heart was pleased" (18:20), and he picks up the sacred objects himself. He moves from one patron to a bigger one, just as he moved from Bethlehem to Micah. Readers in every tradition see in him the hired religious professional who serves whoever pays most. The question "which is better for you" is the only test he applies.

a: My gods that I made, you've taken them
p: Micah's cry recalls Laban's: "why did you steal my gods?" A god you made can be carried off.
b: When Rachel took her father's household gods, Laban chased Jacob and asked, "But why did you steal my gods?" (Genesis 31:30). The same objects, teraphim, appear in both stories. Micah even says "my gods that I made," without hearing the problem. The prophets mock gods that must be carried and cannot save (Isaiah 44:9–20; 46:1–7; Jeremiah 10:5). The narrator makes the same point by letting the robbers walk off with Micah's whole religion.

a: a people quiet and trusting
p: The phrase from 18:7 comes back at the moment of attack. The victims are described with care; the attackers are not praised.
b: The book does not say God gave Laish to Dan, only that the scouts claimed so (18:10). It says twice that Laish was quiet and unsuspecting, and that "there was no rescuer" (18:28). The word is matsil, "one who snatches away"; Moses' song uses it of God, from whose hand no one can rescue (Deuteronomy 32:39; compare Psalm 50:22). Many readers, Jewish and Christian, conclude that the narrator is showing a war of greed dressed as holy war. Niditch calls it a raid on a peaceful people.

a: They gave the town the name Dan
p: The renamed town became Israel's northern limit. "From Dan to Beersheba" came to mean the whole land.
b: The phrase appears in 20:1 and often after (1 Samuel 3:20; 2 Samuel 24:2; 1 Kings 4:25). Joshua 19:47 tells the same renaming with the old name Leshem. Genesis 14:14 already calls the place Dan, which suggests that verse was written or updated after the Danite move.

a: Jonathan, son of Gershom,
t: Moses' grandson at an idol shrine
p: The idol priest of Dan was a direct descendant of Moses. The Hebrew text marks the name with a raised letter.
b: Gershom was Moses' firstborn (Exodus 2:22; 18:3). If "son" means grandson or later descendant, as it often does, Jonathan belonged to Moses' own line. The Talmud says he was Moses' grandson, linked to Manasseh because he acted like the wicked king Manasseh (Bava Batra 109b). Rashi adds that the nun was written raised, turning "Moses" into "Manasseh," out of respect for Moses (see the variant on "Moses"). Jeroboam later set up a golden calf at Dan with priests "who were not Levites" (1 Kings 12:29–31). This verse claims Dan's priesthood came from Moses. Some critical scholars think a priestly family at Dan really traced itself to Moses, and that the story was told against them.

a: until the day the land was taken into exile
p: The note dates the editing of the story: at least as late as the Assyrian conquest of the north, in 733 or 722 BC.
b: Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria took the region of Dan and Naphtali and deported its people about 733 BC (2 Kings 15:29), and Samaria fell in 722 (2 Kings 17:6). Either could be meant. Some scholars, noting that 18:31 speaks of Shiloh, suggest a one-letter change from ha'arets "the land" to ha'aron "the ark," meaning the ark's capture by the Philistines (1 Samuel 4:11). No manuscript reads that. Traditional readers accept that a later prophet or editor added this note to an earlier account.

a: all the time that the house of God stood at Shiloh
t: Shiloh and the end of its shrine
p: Shiloh held the tabernacle and the ark. Its sanctuary ended violently, probably in the mid-1000s BC.
b: Joshua set up the tent of meeting at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1), and Samuel grew up serving there (1 Samuel 1–3). Jeremiah warned Jerusalem to remember what God did to Shiloh (Jeremiah 7:12–14), and Psalm 78:60 says God abandoned it. Danish and Israeli excavations at Khirbet Seilun found a burn layer from the 1000s BC that many link with the Philistine victory of 1 Samuel 4. The verse sets two "houses of God" side by side: the true one at Shiloh and Micah's copy at Dan.

a: In those days, with no king in Israel
p: The story comes last, but it may be one of the earliest in the book. Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, is still priest (20:28).
b: Because Phinehas serves in 20:28 and Moses' grandson in 18:30, many readers, ancient and modern, place chapters 17–21 soon after Joshua. Josephus tells the Gibeah story before any of the judges (Antiquities 5.136–174). Rabbinic chronology (Seder Olam Rabbah, followed by Rashi) puts it at the start of the judges period too. If so, the book has placed its oldest story last, for its theme: this is where the people end up when every man does what is right in his own eyes. Critical scholars often date the writing of these chapters late, while some of the traditions behind them may be old.

a: to be his concubine
p: A pilegesh was a wife of lower rank, not a mistress. The Levite is called her husband and her father his father-in-law.
b: A concubine was legally attached to one man but did not have the full standing of a primary wife; her children might not inherit equally. Abraham, Jacob, Gideon, Saul and David had concubines (Genesis 25:6; 35:22; 8:31; 2 Samuel 3:7; 5:13). The story calls the Levite "her husband" (19:3; 20:4) and her father his "father-in-law" (19:4). Yet she is never named, and the narrator increasingly calls the Levite "her master" (19:26–27). See the topic page.

a: went to her father's house in Bethlehem in Judah
p: The Talmud blames the husband: he made his household afraid of him over a trifle.
b: The Talmud records two rabbis' guesses at what started the quarrel: one says the Levite found a fly in his food, the other a hair; either way, he exploded in anger (Gittin 6b). From this the rabbis drew a lesson: a man should never terrorize his household, because "the concubine of Gibeah" led to the deaths of tens of thousands. Modern readers note that she goes to her father, which a woman guilty of adultery would hardly do, and that her husband goes after her "to speak to her heart" (19:3). See the variant on "broke faith with him."

a: to speak to her heart
p: The phrase means to speak tenderly, to win someone back. The Levite never does it in the story.
b: Shechem "spoke to the girl's heart" after he had violated Dinah (Genesis 34:3). Joseph spoke to his brothers' hearts (Genesis 50:21), Boaz to Ruth's (Ruth 2:13), and God promises to speak to Jerusalem's heart (Isaiah 40:2) and to lead unfaithful Israel into the wilderness and speak to her heart (Hosea 2:14). Trible notes the bitter irony: the Levite goes to speak to her heart, but in the whole story he speaks to her only once, at the door: "Up," and "We're going" (19:28).

a: His father-in-law, the young woman's father, held on to him
p: The father's hospitality is lavish, almost comic. It sets up the cold welcome at Gibeah and the late start that leads there.
b: The scene repeats itself: rise early, be urged to eat, stay. The father may be trying to protect his daughter or to restore his family's honor. Nothing is said of the young woman herself; the men eat and drink and talk. Many readers see the delay as fateful: if they had left on the fourth morning, they would not have reached Gibeah at nightfall. The contrast is sharp: too much hospitality in Bethlehem, none in Gibeah (19:15).

a: Jebus, which is Jerusalem
p: Jerusalem was held by the Jebusites until David took it. Some scholars doubt the city was ever called "Jebus."
b: Judges 1:21 says Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem, and David captured it from them (2 Samuel 5:6–9). Outside the Bible, ancient texts such as the Amarna Letters (1300s BC) call the city Urusalim, never Jebus. J. Maxwell Miller argued that "Jebus" is a later name made from the people's name, the Jebusites. Either way, the city was foreign in this period, about six miles from Bethlehem.

a: We will not turn aside into a town of foreigners, people who are not of Israel.
p: The Levite avoids the foreign city to stay among his own people. His own people are the danger.
b: The irony is bitter and almost every reader notices it. The Jebusites would likely have shown the travelers the hospitality expected of any town. In Gibeah of Benjamin no one takes them in, and the men of the town attack. The story shows Israel behaving worse than the Canaanites it was meant to replace, and worse than Sodom (see the note on 19:22).

a: Gibeah, the town of Benjamin
p: Gibeah, "hill," lay a few miles north of Jerusalem. It would become King Saul's hometown.
b: Most scholars place Gibeah at Tell el-Ful, just north of Jerusalem, where William F. Albright and later Paul Lapp excavated a small fortress. Some place it elsewhere nearby. Saul came from Gibeah, and it was his capital (1 Samuel 10:26; 11:4; 15:34). Readers who see these chapters as a case against Saul's house note that his town is the scene of the crime. Hosea twice calls Israel back to "the days of Gibeah" as a byword for deep corruption (Hosea 9:9; 10:9).
r: 1 Samuel 10:26; 1 Samuel 11:4; 1 Samuel 15:34; Hosea 9:9; Hosea 10:9; Isaiah 10:29

a: but nobody offered to bring them home for the night
p: Travelers without contacts waited in a town's open square. Someone was expected to take them in.
b: With no inns in small towns, hospitality to strangers was a basic duty in Israel and among its neighbors. Abraham ran to meet strangers (Genesis 18:2–8); Lot pressed the two visitors to stay (Genesis 19:2–3). The Levite sits in the square of an Israelite town, and no one comes. Only another outsider, an Ephraimite living in Gibeah as a foreigner (19:16), offers a bed. The law repeatedly commands care for the stranger (Leviticus 19:33–34; Deuteronomy 10:19).
r: Genesis 18:2–8; Genesis 19:2–3; Leviticus 19:33–34; Deuteronomy 10:19; Job 31:32; Hebrews 13:2

a: and was staying in Gibeah as a foreigner
p: Like Lot in Sodom, the only host in Gibeah is himself an outsider.
b: The men of Sodom sneered that Lot "came here to live as a foreigner" (Genesis 19:9). The old man of Gibeah is also from somewhere else, the hill country of Ephraim, the Levite's own region. Stuart Lasine called the chapter "Lot's hospitality in an inverted world": the forms of the Genesis story are all here, but each part is twisted. The note at 19:22 lists the parallels.

a: for me and for your servant woman
p: Out of politeness, the Levite calls his concubine the host's servant. The polite phrase will soon become terribly literal.
b: Calling oneself "your servant" was ordinary courtesy (Genesis 18:3). The Levite extends it to the woman, "your servant woman." Within hours, the host will offer her to the mob as if she were his to give (19:24), and the Levite will push her out himself (19:25). Trible traces how, step by step, the woman is spoken of as property by every man in the story.

a: Bring out the man who came to your house
p: The scene repeats Genesis 19 almost line for line. The writer wants readers to see Gibeah as a new Sodom.
b: Compare the two. Evening arrival and a host who is an outsider (Genesis 19:1, 9; 19:16). Men of the city surround the house (Genesis 19:4). They demand: "Bring them out to us so we can know them" (Genesis 19:5). The host goes out and says, "Please, my brothers, do not do this evil" (Genesis 19:7). He offers two women and says "you can do with them whatever looks good to you" (Genesis 19:8). Then the stories split. In Sodom the angels pull Lot in and strike the mob blind (Genesis 19:10–11). In Gibeah no one intervenes, and the woman is thrown out. Israel has become Sodom, and there are no angels.

a: so we can know him
p: Yada' means to know, and also to have sex with. The mob means rape. The next verses leave no doubt.
b: Genesis uses yada' for sexual union (Genesis 4:1). Here, as in Genesis 19:5, the men demand to "know" the guest, and the host's reply ("do not do evil," "this disgraceful thing") shows what they mean. In 19:25 "they knew her" describes the gang rape. The crime is violent humiliation of an outsider, not a relationship. This bears on the modern debate over what these stories say about same-sex relations: many interpreters, conservative and liberal, agree the passages condemn rape and the violation of hospitality; they disagree on whether they also address consensual relations.

a: worthless men
p: Bene beliyya'al means good-for-nothings or scoundrels. Later the word Belial became a name for Satan.
b: The phrase describes those who lead Israel to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:13), Eli's corrupt sons (1 Samuel 2:12), and the men who sneered at Saul (1 Samuel 10:27). Beliyya'al probably means "without worth" or "no rising," though its origin is debated. By the time of the Dead Sea Scrolls, Belial was the name of the chief evil spirit, and Paul uses it for Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15).

a: do not do this disgraceful thing.
