p: Nevalah is a crime that breaks the community's basic decency, especially sexual outrage. It returns in 20:6 and 20:10.
b: Nevalah comes from the same root as naval, a godless fool (Psalm 14:1). It is used for the rape of Dinah, "a disgraceful thing in Israel" (Genesis 34:7), for a bride's hidden unchastity (Deuteronomy 22:21), and for Amnon's rape of Tamar (2 Samuel 13:12). The host uses the word for the attack on his male guest, and then offers the women as if what was done to them would not be the same thing.

a: Here is my daughter, the virgin, and his concubine.
p: To protect a male guest, the host offers his own daughter and the guest's wife. How should readers judge him?
b: Some traditional readers explain the offer by the ancient code of hospitality, in which a guest's safety came before almost anything; they still call it wrong. Many others, including Block, see the host as no better than Lot, and the narrator as showing how low Israel's men have sunk. Feminist readers, especially Phyllis Trible and J. Cheryl Exum, stress that the women are treated as objects to be traded between men, and that the text lets us hear the men's voices but never the women's. All agree the text offers no word of approval.

a: Dishonor them
p: 'Innah means to humble, violate or abuse. Here it can only mean rape.
b: The verb 'innah covers a range: to oppress (Exodus 1:11), to humble oneself by fasting (Leviticus 16:29), to shame a woman by sex outside proper bounds (Deuteronomy 22:24, 29), and to force her (Genesis 34:2; 2 Samuel 13:14). The verb itself does not say whether force was used; context decides. In this verse the context is a mob at the door. The same word described what the Philistines wanted to do to Samson (16:5) and what the Levite says was done to his concubine (20:5).

a: So the man seized his concubine and brought her outside to them.
p: "The man" could be the host or the Levite. Most readers take it as the Levite.
b: The Hebrew says only "the man took hold of his concubine." "His concubine" points to the Levite, whose concubine she was. The verb "seized" (vayyachazeq) is the same one used when the Levite cuts her up in 19:29. In his speech at Mizpah (20:5), the Levite leaves this out. Some readers think the host acted; most take it as the Levite saving himself by giving up his wife. The text does not say whether she struggled or spoke. She is not given a single word in the whole story.

a: abused her all night until morning
p: Hit'allel means to deal harshly with someone, to make a plaything of them, as enemies do with captives.
b: The verb hit'allel be- is used of God's dealings with Egypt (Exodus 10:2), of Saul's fear that the Philistines would "make sport" of him if captured (1 Samuel 31:4), and of Balaam's donkey making a fool of him (Numbers 22:29). Here it describes a night-long gang rape. The narrator's language is restrained, with no detail. Trible's title for her study of this chapter is "An Unnamed Woman: The Extravagance of Violence."

a: where her master was
p: At the start the Levite is "her husband." Now the narrator calls him "her master."
b: In 19:3 he set out as "her husband" (ishah). In 19:26–27 he is "her master" (adoneyha), the word used for owners of slaves. Trible and others see the shift as the narrator's quiet verdict on how the Levite treats her. The word can also be a respectful title for a husband (Genesis 18:12), so some read less into it. Even so, the timing is telling: she lies at the door of the house where "her master" sleeps.

a: with her hands on the threshold
p: She reached the door of the house where she might have found safety, and no further.
b: The threshold is the line between the safety of the house and the danger outside. Her hands are stretched toward it. Many readers see a silent plea; Trible dwells on this image. The Levite opens the door "to go his way" (that is, to leave), which suggests he did not go looking for her.

a: He lifted her onto the donkey
p: The Hebrew does not say whether she was dead when he cut her up. The Greek does.
b: The Hebrew says only that she did not answer. The Septuagint adds "for she was dead" (see the variant on "No one answered."). Without that addition, the reader is left with a horrible possibility: that she was still alive when the Levite "took the knife" (19:29). Trible and Bal raise the question; the Levite's later claim that the men of Gibeah killed her (20:4–5) is his version. Traditional readers generally assume she died at the door. The Hebrew's silence leaves the question open, and many think it is meant to.

a: took the knife
p: The word for knife, ma'akhelet, appears elsewhere only for Abraham's knife at the binding of Isaac and once in Proverbs.
b: "The knife" has the definite article, as if it were a known knife. Ma'akhelet appears in Genesis 22:6 and 22:10, where Abraham "took hold of the knife to slaughter his son" (Genesis 22:10), and in Proverbs 30:14. Many readers think the echo is deliberate. At Moriah, God stopped the knife; at Gibeah, no one does. The verb for "cut her up" (nittach) is the word for cutting up a sacrificial animal (Exodus 29:17; Leviticus 1:6).

a: into twelve pieces
t: Twelve pieces sent to twelve tribes
p: A grisly summons to war. Saul will do the same with oxen to call Israel out to rescue Jabesh-gilead.
b: Saul cut a yoke of oxen into pieces and sent them through Israel with the threat that anyone who did not come would have his oxen treated the same (1 Samuel 11:7). A letter from the Mari archive (1700s BC; ARM 2.48) suggests cutting off a criminal's head and parading it through the towns to make troops come out. The twelve pieces stand for the twelve tribes, compare Ahijah's cloak torn into twelve (1 Kings 11:30). The irony is deep: Saul, from Gibeah, will rescue Jabesh, which Israel destroyed in 21:10.

a: Set your minds on it, talk it over, and speak out!
p: Israel never forgot this crime. Hosea uses it as a byword for corruption centuries later.
b: Hosea says, "They have gone deep in their corruption, as in the days of Gibeah" (Hosea 9:9, fresh rendering), and "Since the days of Gibeah, Israel, you have sinned" (Hosea 10:9). Whether Hosea means this story or an event in Saul's reign is debated, but most think this one. The call "set your minds on it" (literally, "set it on yourselves") is also a call to readers: the story is meant to be thought about, not skipped.

a: The community came together like one man
p: Israel is never so united in Judges as here, and the unity is used to destroy one of its own tribes.
b: The phrase "like one man" appears in 20:1, 8 and 11. In the judges stories, tribes often failed to come (5:15–17; 8:1; 12:1). Here every tribe gathers from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south, even from Gilead across the Jordan (but see 21:8). Readers note the irony: the only war in Judges that all Israel fights together is a civil war. The "community" ('edah) is the word used of Israel assembled in the wilderness (Numbers 1:2).

a: at Mizpah
p: Mizpah, "Watchtower," was a meeting place on Benjamin's land. It is usually identified with Tell en-Nasbeh, north of Jerusalem.
b: This Mizpah is not the Mizpah of Gilead in Jephthah's story (11:29, 34). Samuel later gathered Israel here (1 Samuel 7:5–6; 10:17), and after Jerusalem fell it became the seat of Judah's governor (2 Kings 25:23; Jeremiah 40:6). Gathering in Benjamin's own territory was itself a message to Benjamin.

a: four hundred thousand men on foot, drawing the sword
p: Four hundred thousand men would be a huge army for this period. Some scholars think 'elef here means a unit, not a thousand.
b: The Hebrew 'elef means "thousand" but can also mean a clan or a military unit (as in 6:15, "my clan"). George Mendenhall proposed that the large numbers in the census lists counted units rather than individuals. On that view, "four hundred 'elef" would be four hundred units of a few men each. Traditional readers often take the numbers as given. Others take them as round figures that show the size of the disaster. The losses in this chapter (22,000; 18,000; 25,000) raise the same question.

a: The pillars of the whole people
p: Pinnot means corners or cornerstones. Here it means the leaders who hold the people together.
b: The same image appears in 1 Samuel 14:38 ("All you cornerstones of the people") and Isaiah 19:13 ("the corner pillars of its tribes"). Psalm 118:22 calls the rejected stone the "head of the corner." The Plain English Translation uses "pillars" to give the sense of leaders on whom the whole people rests.

a: Me they meant to kill, and my concubine they dishonored, and she died.
p: His account leaves out that he handed her over and says nothing of how she died or what he did with the knife.
b: Compare 19:22–29. The men asked for him "so we can know him"; he says they meant to kill him. He says nothing about pushing her out the door. He says "she died," leaving the impression the men killed her. Commentators of every school notice the gaps. Traditional readers such as Block call his speech self-serving. Feminist readers (Trible, Exum, Bal) see the whole public war that follows as built on a man's edited story. Some readers defend him in part: perhaps he truly feared death, and perhaps she was dead when he found her.

a: because they committed a vile act, a disgraceful thing in Israel
p: Zimmah is a word for depraved sexual sin; nevalah is the outrage against decency (see 19:23).
b: Zimmah names the worst sexual crimes in Leviticus (Leviticus 18:17; 20:14) and wicked schemes (Psalm 26:10). Together with nevalah it marks what was done as a crime against the whole people, "in Israel." The phrase "a disgraceful thing in Israel" (Genesis 34:7) was used for the rape of Dinah too. In both stories the brothers' response goes far beyond the guilty.

a: we will go up against it as the lot directs
p: Israel uses the lot to decide who goes. Earlier, lots divided the land among the tribes.
b: Casting lots was a way of letting God decide (Proverbs 16:33). It was used to divide the land (Joshua 18:6–10) and to find the guilty (Joshua 7:14–18; 1 Samuel 14:41–42). Here it chooses the troops, perhaps the one in ten who bring supplies (20:10). The Hebrew is clipped, "against it, by lot"; the Greek supplies "we will go up," as the Plain English Translation does.

a: Gibeah of Benjamin
p: The Hebrew here says "Geba of Benjamin," a nearby town with almost the same name. Most think Gibeah is meant.
b: Geba and Gibeah both mean "hill" and were two different towns a few miles apart, often confused even in the Hebrew (compare 1 Samuel 13:3, 16). The Plain English Translation reads "Gibeah," as the KJV and most translations do, because the whole story is about Gibeah. In 20:33 the Plain English Translation keeps "Geba," because there the name belongs to a stretch of ground and the Greek texts disagree (see the variant there).

a: sweep the evil out of Israel
p: The words come from Deuteronomy's laws: the guilty must be punished so the evil is removed from the community.
b: Deuteronomy repeats the formula "sweep the evil out from among you" after laws on idolatry, murder and sexual crimes (Deuteronomy 13:5; 17:7; 22:21–24). Israel's first demand is just and limited: hand over the guilty men. Benjamin's refusal puts tribal loyalty above justice, and turns a crime by some into a war on all. Readers across traditions see both sides failing: Benjamin by shielding the guilty, Israel by what it does next.

a: seven hundred picked men were hampered in the right hand
t: Left-handed slingers from the "son of the right hand"
p: Their right hand was "bound": they fought left-handed, like Ehud. Benjamin means "son of the right hand."
b: The phrase itter yad-yemino is used of Ehud the Benjaminite in 3:15. It may describe men trained from childhood to fight left-handed, which made them hard to guard against. 1 Chronicles 12:2 describes Benjaminite warriors who could sling stones with either hand. The irony of left-handers in the tribe of the "right hand" (Binyamin) is often noted. Slingstones the size of a fist are found at many Iron Age battle sites; slings were deadly weapons (1 Samuel 17:49).

a: never missing
p: The verb is chata', the Bible's usual word for sin. Its first sense is to miss the mark.
b: Chata' is the most common Hebrew word for sin, but its plain sense is to miss a target or lose the way (compare Proverbs 19:2, where someone in a hurry "misses the way"). Here it has that plain sense: these slingers never missed. Many readers hear the irony. The tribe that will not hand over the guilty men of Gibeah, and so takes their sin on itself, is the tribe whose men "never miss."

a: Which of us should go up first to do battle with the Benjaminites?
t: The book's first question asked again
p: Judges opened by asking who would go first against the Canaanites. Now the enemy is a brother tribe.
b: In 1:1–2 the Israelites asked the LORD who would go up first against the Canaanites, and the answer was Judah. Here the question and the answer are the same, but the enemy is Benjamin. The book has come full circle, and the circle is a downward one. The place is Bethel, "house of God"; the KJV translates the name there and in 20:26 and 21:2.

a: Shall I come near again for battle with the Benjaminites, my brother?
t: Why does God let them lose?
p: God tells Israel to attack, and Israel loses forty thousand men in two days. Readers have offered several explanations.
b: Some say Israel asked only how, never whether, and never repented of its own sins; only after the second defeat do they fast and offer sacrifices (20:26). The Talmud says Israel was punished because it rose up for the honor of a human being, the concubine, but never protested Micah's idol, an offense to God's honor (Sanhedrin 103b); Pseudo-Philo tells the story in a similar way (Biblical Antiquities 45–47). Others see God judging the whole nation, not just Benjamin. Critical scholars often see older battle tradition reworked to make a theological point. The question "my brother" shows that Israel itself has begun to feel the horror.

a: The ark of the covenant of God was there in those days
p: This is the only mention of the ark in Judges. Here it is at Bethel, not at Shiloh.
b: Elsewhere the ark and tabernacle are at Shiloh (18:31; Joshua 18:1; 1 Samuel 4:3). The ark may have been brought to Bethel for the war, as it was later taken into battle (1 Samuel 4:3–4). Or the Hebrew beit-el may be read "the house of God" (as the KJV does in 20:26), meaning wherever the sanctuary stood. Either way, the verse explains how Israel could consult God here.

a: Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, served before it in those days
p: Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, was a young man in the wilderness. So this war took place within a generation of Joshua.
b: Phinehas killed an Israelite and a Midianite woman at Peor and was promised a lasting priesthood (Numbers 25:7–13). He led the delegation to the eastern tribes in Joshua 22. His presence here is the clearest sign that chapters 19–21 happened early, though they come last. His zeal at Peor stopped a plague; here he consults God for a war that nearly wipes out a tribe.

a: So Israel posted men in hiding all around Gibeah
t: The ambush of Ai, used on Israelites
p: Israel defeats Gibeah with the same trick Joshua used at Ai: fake retreat, hidden troops, a burning city.
b: At Ai, Joshua set an ambush behind the city, drew its men out by pretending to flee, and the ambush entered and burned the city; the smoke was the signal (Joshua 8:3–22). Every step is repeated here. The tactics of holy war against Canaan are now used against a tribe of Israel. Niditch and others see this as the narrator's point: Israel has turned the conquest inward.

a: on the highways (one goes up to Bethel, the other to Gibeah)
p: The roads lead to Bethel and to "Gibeah in the field," yet the battle is at Gibeah. Some suggest another place was meant.
b: The fight is taking place near Gibeah, so a road "going up to Gibeah" is odd. Some scholars read "Gibeon," a town to the west, or understand another hill (giv'ah) in the countryside. The KJV translates Bethel as "the house of God" here. The general picture is clear: two roads north from Gibeah, where the Benjaminites chase the Israelites into a trap.

a: The LORD routed Benjamin in front of Israel
p: 20:29–36 tells the victory in summary; 20:36–48 tells it again in detail. The numbers leave a thousand men unaccounted for.
b: Many critical scholars see two sources combined. Others see a common Hebrew way of telling: a summary first, then the full account (as in Genesis 1 and 2). Most of the numbers fit: 25,100 dead in 20:35 is rounded to 25,000 in 20:46, which is 18,000 + 5,000 + 2,000 (20:44–45). But 25,100 dead and 600 survivors (20:47) make 25,700, while the Hebrew of 20:15 counts 26,700. One Greek text reads 25,000 in 20:15, which makes the sums agree exactly; it may be a correction made for that reason (see the variant on 20:15). Some literary scholars argue that the retelling builds suspense rather than showing careless editing.

a: there was the whole town going up toward the sky
p: The Hebrew kalil, "the whole town," is the word for an offering burned entire. Gibeah is treated like a town under the ban.
b: Kalil means "whole" and is the term for an offering burned completely (Leviticus 6:22; Deuteronomy 33:10). Deuteronomy commands that a town of Israel that turns to other gods be burned "as a whole offering to the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 13:16). Gibeah's sin was not idolatry, but Israel treats it the same way. Benjamin looks back and sees its town going up like smoke from an altar.

a: Six hundred men turned and fled toward the wilderness, to the Rock of Rimmon
p: The Rock of Rimmon is a limestone hill east of Bethel, with caves. Six hundred men are all that is left of a tribe.
b: The site is usually identified with the village of Rammun, about four miles east of Bethel, on a rocky hill with caves. Six hundred is the same number as the Danite war band (18:11, 16), and Saul's band will later number six hundred (1 Samuel 13:15; 14:2). The men stay four months, as long as the concubine stayed with her father (19:2). Everything in chapter 21 depends on these survivors.

a: They put them to the sword, town after town, people and animals
p: Israel destroys Benjamin's towns, people and animals, as if Benjamin were a Canaanite city under the ban.
b: The Hebrew is hard ("from the city, men [or 'entire'], to beast"), but the picture is total destruction. This is the treatment the law ordered for Canaanite towns (Deuteronomy 20:16–17) and for an Israelite town gone over to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:15). Israel's anger outruns its law: the guilty were a few men of Gibeah (20:13). Niditch reads the war as a picture of what "holy war" thinking does when turned inward. Traditional readers see judgment on Benjamin carried beyond what God commanded.

a: Now the men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah
p: We learn only now that Israel swore not to give daughters to Benjamin. Like Jephthah's vow, it binds them to harm.
b: Rash oaths run through Judges and Samuel: Jephthah's vow (11:30–31) and Saul's curse on anyone who ate (1 Samuel 14:24). The law took oaths very seriously (Numbers 30:2), and Israel will not break this one. Instead the elders find ways around it that cost other people their lives and freedom. Ecclesiastes warns, "Do not rush to open your mouth" (Ecclesiastes 5:2), and Jesus taught that oaths should not be needed at all (Matthew 5:33–37).

a: O LORD, God of Israel, what has made this happen in Israel
p: Israel weeps and asks God why a tribe is missing. The reader knows why: Israel did it.
b: The question sounds like lament, but the answer is plain from chapter 20. 21:15 goes further and says "the LORD had torn a gap." Readers differ on the tone. Many see sincere grief that comes too late. Others hear self-deception: the people speak as if events happened to them. Webb notes that God does not answer this question; there is no oracle in chapter 21 at all. The elders work out the rest by themselves.

a: He must surely be put to death.
p: Another oath, mentioned only now, makes Jabesh-gilead the target. One oath is solved by enforcing the other.
b: The first oath (no daughters for Benjamin) creates a problem; the second oath (death for anyone who did not come) supplies the answer. Many readers note how neatly the second oath serves the leaders' need, and wonder whether it was used as a pretext. Saul later threatened those who did not come out (1 Samuel 11:7). Here the threat is carried out on a whole town.

a: from Jabesh-gilead
p: Jabesh lay east of the Jordan. Its fate here is tied to Saul's story: Saul rescues it, and its men bury him.
b: Jabesh-gilead was probably on the Wadi Yabis, east of the Jordan; its exact site is debated. In 1 Samuel 11 Saul's first act as king is to save Jabesh from the Ammonites; when Saul dies, the men of Jabesh risk their lives to give him burial (1 Samuel 31:11–13). This chapter gives a family reason: many of Benjamin's wives came from Jabesh. Readers who see a pro-David purpose in Judges 19–21 point out that Saul's tribe, town and allies all appear in a bad light here.

a: every male, and every woman who has lain with a man, you are to put under the ban
p: The order echoes Moses' order after the war on Midian: kill the women who have slept with a man, and keep the girls.
b: In Numbers 31:17–18 Moses commanded, "kill every woman who has slept with a man" (Numbers 31:17), and the young girls were kept alive. The order here follows that pattern, applied to an Israelite town. Cherem, "the ban," was meant for Canaan (Deuteronomy 7:2; 20:17). Here it is turned on Israelites, and its purpose is to supply wives. Feminist readers (Bal, Exum) see women's bodies used to solve men's political problems from 19:24 to 21:23. Traditional readers see the logic of the book's ending: Israel acts without God's word and calls it law.

a: Shiloh in the land of Canaan
p: A strange note: Shiloh was in the middle of Israel. The phrase may simply contrast it with Gilead across the Jordan.
b: The Hebrew of Joshua 22:9 has the same phrase ("at Shiloh in the land of Canaan" on this site) to contrast the western land with Gilead in the east. Some readers also hear a darker meaning: Israel now behaves like the Canaanites, so its holy place lies in "Canaan." The detail in 21:19 about where Shiloh is located suggests the narrator wrote for readers who no longer knew the town, perhaps after it was destroyed (see the note on 18:31).

a: The LORD had made a breach in the tribes of Israel.
p: Perets is a breach, a gap in a wall. The people say the LORD made it.
b: Perets is used of a broken wall (Nehemiah 6:1) and of God "breaking out" against Uzzah (2 Samuel 6:8). The people say the LORD made the breach. In a sense he did: he sent Israel against Benjamin (20:28). But the killing of women and children was Israel's own doing (20:48). The verse holds both: God's judgment and human excess.

a: Benjamin's survivors must keep their holding
p: Literally "a possession of escape for Benjamin": the survivors must keep the tribe's land, or have heirs.
b: The words yerushat peletah leVinyamin are compressed. Some read "the survivors must keep Benjamin's inheritance"; others, changing the vowels, "How can a remnant be left for Benjamin?" The concern is the same either way: a tribe without heirs loses its land and vanishes from Israel, as Numbers 27 and 36 also worry about families. The elders' goal is good. Their method is the problem.

a: the LORD's festival is held year by year at Shiloh
p: Probably the autumn grape harvest festival, later called Booths. The Mishnah remembers girls dancing in the vineyards.
b: Vineyards and dancing suggest the end of the grape harvest, the Feast of Booths (Deuteronomy 16:13–15), or a local wine festival. Elkanah went up "year by year" to Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:3, 7). The Mishnah says that on the 15th of Av and on the Day of Atonement the daughters of Jerusalem went out in white clothes to dance in the vineyards, and young men chose brides (Mishnah Taanit 4:8). The Talmud adds that the 15th of Av was the day Benjamin was allowed to marry into the other tribes again (Bavli Taanit 30b).

a: When you see the daughters of Shiloh coming out to dance in the circle dances
p: Women came out with dances to celebrate. Jephthah's daughter came out dancing and was taken too.
b: The mecholot were women's circle dances: Miriam led them at the sea (Exodus 15:20), Jephthah's daughter came out dancing to meet her father (11:34), and women danced for Saul and David (1 Samuel 18:6). Here the dance at a festival of the LORD becomes the hunting ground for abduction. Ackerman and others trace how the women of Judges move from warriors and leaders (Deborah, Jael) to victims and captives at the end.

a: Each of you grab a wife for himself from the daughters of Shiloh
p: Roman legend tells how Rome's first men seized brides at a festival. The likeness to Shiloh is striking.
b: The historian Livy (History of Rome 1.9) tells how Romulus, his city lacking women, invited the neighboring Sabines to a festival and had his men carry off their daughters. The parallels are clear: a people short of wives, a festival, a planned seizure, and an appeal to the fathers afterward. Most scholars think the two are independent stories of a common kind, since bride-capture is known in many cultures. No borrowing in either direction can be shown.

a: Be gracious to us about them.
p: The elders' answer to the fathers is a legal trick: you did not give your daughters, they were taken, so you broke no oath.
b: The Hebrew is difficult, but the argument seems to be: (1) be gracious, (2) we could not find enough wives in the war at Jabesh, (3) you are not guilty of breaking the oath, because you did not give them. The oath is kept in letter and broken in spirit. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers have usually seen here the confusion of a people without a king or a word from God. Feminist readers, among them Exum and Bal, point out that no one asks the young women anything. The six hundred are "wives" by force.

a: built the towns up again and lived there
p: The tribe lives on. From it will come Saul, Israel's first king, and much later Paul.
b: Benjamin recovered and became small but proud (Psalm 68:27). Its sons included Saul (1 Samuel 9:1–2), Mordecai (Esther 2:5) and Paul, who twice names his tribe (Romans 11:1; Philippians 3:5). After the north split away, Benjamin stayed with Judah (1 Kings 12:21), and the two together became the Jewish people of later times. The book that nearly lost a tribe ends with it rebuilt, though by deeply wrong means.
r: 1 Samuel 9:1–2; Psalm 68:27; Esther 2:5; 1 Kings 12:21; Romans 11:1; Philippians 3:5

a: Everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes.
p: Judges ends with its refrain, not a verdict. What comes next in the Bible shapes how readers hear it.
b: In the Hebrew Bible, 1 Samuel follows: the birth of Samuel, the call for a king, and Saul and David. Read that way, the refrain sets up the monarchy (see the note on 17:6). In Christian Bibles, following the Greek order, Ruth comes next, set "In the days when the judges ruled" (Ruth 1:1). It is a story of loyalty and kindness in Bethlehem, the hometown of the first Levite and of the concubine, ending with the birth of David's grandfather. Readers have long noticed how Ruth answers the darkness of Judges 19–21.
